title: DFS on San Francisco Streets: Trail First ⚡
description: Watch DFS traverse real city-style street intersections, diving deep along one route before backtracking when it hits dead ends. In this visualization, you’ll see how stack behavior turns “find a path” into a deterministic graph exploration.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — What happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡

In this street-graph visualization, each intersection is a node and each road segment is an edge. DFS (Depth First Search) uses a stack/recursion to “go as deep as possible” following an adjacency order, then backtracks when it can’t move forward.

Key moments you’ll spot:
• Deep dive: it commits to a branch instead of searching level-by-level (unlike BFS)
• Backtracking: dead ends trigger pops/returns to the last choice point
• Deterministic pathing: the exploration order depends on how neighbors are ordered

Takeaway: DFS is a powerful graph traversal (and the backbone of many graph/maze problems), but it won’t guarantee the shortest path—only the first found path under the chosen neighbor ordering.

Debate question: If DFS finds *any* valid route, should real routing prefer “first found” speed or “shortest path” certainty?
